extracted.intended_audience: readers of an early-18th-century periodical interested in theatre, manners, and public affairs (general literate public)
extracted.subtask_description: Short, public-facing essays and criticisms about theatre, acting, social types, and contemporary manners — assessing performances, dramatic writing, and social practices with examples and anecdotes. The text mixes theatrical criticism, satiric social taxonomy, and moral commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting: nature excellently represented; avoid 'doing too much'
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘There is certainly nature excellently represented in his manner of action; in which he ever avoided that general fault in players, of doing too much.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise for a manner of acting that faithfully represents nature and shows restraint. Implies that overacting is a common fault; the preferred approach is naturalness and measured expression rather than exaggerated affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actors should not 'add to his authors' (avoid inserting original lines)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘He has not the merit of some ingenious persons now on the stage, of adding to his authors; for the actors were so dull in the last age, that many of them have gone out of the world, without having ever spoke one word of their own in the theatre.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit standard that actors ought not to alter or augment the author's text with their own words. The passage contrasts plain delivery (virtue) with later actors who insert or improvise, treating fidelity to the play as a merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose parts suitable to the actor's stage and condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: the actor 'pretends only to act a part fit for a man who has one foot in the grave; viz., a gravedigger.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select roles appropriate to an actor's persona, age, or physicality — playing characters that fit the performer's natural appearance or life-stage is preferable to forced mismatches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for new comedies via subscription to improve public diversion
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘There is actually a subscription made by many persons of wit and quality, for the encouragement of new comedies. This design will very much contribute to the improvement and diversion of the town.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social/institutional criterion: patronage (subscriptions) for new dramatic works is recommended as a means to improve theatrical quality and public entertainment; implies that funding and encouragement shape artistic improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy writing often follows a predictable, formulaic design
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘I won't pretend to give you an account of the plot, it being the same design upon which all tragedies have been writ for several years last past… from the beginning of the first scene, the frequenters of the house may know, as well as the author, when the battle is to be fought, the lady to yield, and the hero to proceed to his wedding and coronation.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of conventional tragedy: predictable tropes (farewell of general, dying for love, politician's confession, heroic coronation) indicate a lack of originality. Anti-pattern: using stock devices that make outcomes obvious to audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedian's mechanical performance as symptom of formulaic drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire: an 'eminent tragedian very much my friend, who shall come in, and go through the whole five acts, without troubling me for one sentence…'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an actor can perform without reference to distinctive lines or dramatic specificity, it signals that the play is mechanically constructed; quality drama should require precise verbal and emotional work from actors, not mere stock gestures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence in 'still-life' comic characters (stiff/heavy/stupid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Underhill's particular excellence was 'in characters that may be called still-life; I mean the stiff, the heavy, and the stupid; to these he gave the exactest and most expressive colours… A countenance of wood could not be more fixed than his…'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A standard for comic acting: success in portraying inert, lumpish, or moping characters through precise, restrained facial and physical expression. Shows that different comic types require distinct skills (subtlety, restraint) rather than broad buffoonery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and qualities of a 'Very Pretty Fellow' (social character type)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'Very Pretty Fellow' is exalted above a 'Pretty Fellow' by peculiar sprightliness: jaunty behaviour, careless of offending, sanguine, familiarly nicknamed, protected by women, errors passed over, admitted everywhere, and whose faults doubly please when he succeeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A typology used to evaluate social/character virtues: sprightliness, spontaneity, and being of 'no consequence' are praised as ingredients of social success. Examples (Colonel Brunett) and anti-patterns (affected imitation) are provided to show what does and doesn't make the type authentic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bacchanalian/celebrated drinking-ability as a recognisable masculine character
rubrics_metrics.description: Three brothers from Holland given nicknames (Hogshead, Culverin, Musket) measured by drinking capacity; superiority judged by liquid weight and power of drinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirical social metric: in certain circles, prowess at drinking functions as a basis for reputation. The passage both defines and mock-evaluates this criterion, warning of excess (Hogshead may be too full).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and social rules for a 'Toast' (female object of public drinking-honour)
rubrics_metrics.description: A toast has a 'joyous and cheerful import'; origin anecdote from Bath; now elevated to a 'formal order' elected by balloting, reigning for a year, name written with a diamond on a drinking-glass to mark her imaginary value and frailty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social-institutional standard: being a 'toast' involves public selection, symbolic accoutrements (diamond on glass), and a temporally-limited honour. Guidance includes the ritualistic inauguration and cautions about the toast's fragile status — commentary on fashion and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of duels: 'satisfaction' as a misleading term; duels are imposture
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay questions the notion of 'satisfaction' and asserts duels are 'an imposture, made up of cowardice, falsehood, and want of understanding.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative standard for judging duelling: rather than honoring participants, duels often expose vanity, false bravado, and irrationality. The author proposes historical comparison and argument to discourage the practice; anti-pattern: equating willingness to be violent with genuine honour.

rubrics_metrics.name: On giving advice: be cautious—people often ask counsel after deciding
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Among the many employments I am necessarily put upon by my friends, that of giving advice is the most unwelcome… some people will ask counsel of you, when they have already acted what they tell you is still under deliberation.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guideline for advisers: use artful responses, recognize when counsel is sought merely as a social ritual rather than for decision-making. Example technique: evasive or strategic answers (e.g., feigned preference) can avoid conflict when the asker has already resolved their choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feigned illness/fits as a social/manipulative tactic (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: A woman governs her husband by 'falling into fits whenever she was repulsed in a request, or contradicted in a discourse,' using staged convulsions to control him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This passage describes and implicitly condemns manipulative social tactics: theatricalized illness as a method of coercion. As guidance, it serves as an example of dishonest social strategy and a warning about such practices in domestic relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social success often depends on perceived opinion and place rather than intrinsic merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that the colonel is 'admitted in one place, because he is so in another; and every man treats Brunett well, not out of his particular esteem for him, but in respect to the opinion of others.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sociological standard for evaluating reputation: acceptance and advancement can be contingent on popular perception and network effects rather than personal merit. Implication: reputation is socially constructed and self-reinforcing.
